REALIZATION CALCULUS
CORE SERIES I
Projector Resolved Seed Calculus I
Typed operator systems, seed rank, and exact packet coordinates
Komorebi P.
Monograph edition
Release edition / 15 October 2026
Overview
This paper begins with a practical mathematical question. Once a family of operators has been
fixed, what can we generate from a few starting vectors, and how can we keep track of the resulting
object? The answer has two parts. Seed rank measures how many starting vectors are needed. Packet
coordinates describe the components of vectors and the transfers between them.
The construction starts with a typed operator grammar and a concrete realization of that gram-
mar. From there we study generated hulls, presentations by seeds and relations, and the number of
generators required by a module. The generator results include reduction modulo the Jacobson rad-
ical, the semisimple multiplicity formula over division rings, and the formula for a single operator
over an arbitrary field.
We then resolve vectors and operators using complete families of idempotents. Finite packet re-
construction is exact. Countable reconstruction requires the stated convergence assumptions. Trans-
fer blocks record the action from each input packet to each output packet, and their multiplication
exposes both admissible paths and cancellation. Later sections develop quotient descent, coordinate
changes, completion, and transport through realization functors.
Worked quiver, coordinate ring, matrix, graph, and shift models show how the same language
is used in different settings. The visual atlas follows these models through complete calculations.
Stable statement identifiers connect this text to the existing machine companion, while the sepa-
rate Lean guide specifies the scope of the formal certificates. The written proofs and the imported
classical results retain their stated hypotheses.

A route through this section
The argument has four stages. Reading them in order makes the later examples easier to follow.
1. Grammar and realization. Specify which compositions of operators are legal, then distinguish
that abstract syntax from the operators that actually act on a chosen space.
2. Generation. Choose one or more seeds and ask which part of the realization is generated by
their operator orbits. The minimal number of required seeds is the seed rank.
3. Packet coordinates. Resolve the space by a complete family of idempotents. Every vector and
every operator then has exact packet coordinates.
4. Transport. Study how those coordinates behave under products, graphs, morphisms, quo-
tients, completion, and realization functors.
The first two layers describe what can be generated. The last two describe how the generated object
is resolved and transported.
The basic conceptual chain
typed grammar ⟶realized algebra ⟶seed hull
⟶seed rank ⟶packet coordinates
⟶transfer blocks ⟶functorial realization.
Each object in this chain has a different role. A grammar is a presentation of allowed operator words.
A realized algebra is the image of that grammar in an endomorphism algebra. A seed hull is an orbit
span inside one particular module. A packet system is an exact coordinate decomposition and need
not be orthogonal. A realization functor is required to preserve a declared mathematical profile, not
merely the vocabulary.

Scope of the argument
The paper does not claim that every useful decomposition is automatically discovered, that ev-
ery packet split is numerically stable, or that exact coordinates solve a nonlinear problem. Paper I
establishes the linear language and its exact transport laws. Refinement, obstruction theory, non-
linear trees, arithmetic valuations, and continuum limits belong to later papers.
1 Coefficient conventions, logical status, and scope
A route through this section
This section sets out the conventions used throughout the paper. It explains when a statement
concerns algebra, when topology enters the argument, which results are taken as classical input,
and how the stable record IDs connect this paper to later work. Keeping these settings distinct
makes the hypotheses of each result easier to follow.
1.1 Ambient regimes and theorem records
Definition 1.1 (Coefficient and module regimes). All modules are left modules unless stated oth-
erwise. The algebraic regime consists of a unital ring 𝐴and a unital left module 𝑀over 𝐴. When
linear dimensions, tensor products, quivers, or operator blocks are used, 𝐴is a unital algebra
over 𝕜, where 𝕜is a field, and 𝑀is a vector space over 𝕜. The topological regime consists of a
Hausdorff topological vector space over a complete valued field, together with a unital algebra
of continuous linear operators. Every infinite sum, completion, quotient topology, and closure
below is interpreted only in the regime explicitly declared in its statement.
Conventions for empty families.
For finite families of nonnegative integers we use max ∅= 0. The
height of an empty finite partially ordered set is 0, as is the height of a nonempty poset with no strict
comparable pair. Thus the height in the theorem for the support preorder counts strict steps.
Definition 1.2 (Canonical theorem record). A canonical theorem record is the tuple
(ID, status, hypotheses, statement, dependencies, proof, exports, boundary).
A downstream paper cites the stable record ID. A domain specialization may add domain hy-
potheses, but it does not repeat a generic proof from this paper.
Boundary 1.3 (Symbolic scope). This edition proves the algebraic and topological statements printed
below. It does not assert historical novelty, independent external certification, automatic discovery of
useful packet systems, nonlinear obstruction theory, multilevel refinement, arithmetic congruences,
quantum gravity, automorphy, or local or global Langlands reciprocity.
2 Typed operator grammars, realizations, and seed systems
A route through this section
An operator grammar describes which compositions are allowed and which relations they satisfy.
A realization gives this syntax a concrete action on vector spaces. Its realized algebra consists of
the operators that actually occur in that action. We can then ask which vectors serve as seeds.

How to read the result
The equivalence does not claim that a quiver presentation is unique. It says that once a grammar is
fixed, working with typed arrows and working with a module over the quotient path algebra carry
the same information. The typed description is often easier for constructing an operator system.
The module description is often easier for proving generation and quotient theorems.

The central idea
Replacing the abstract grammar algebra by its image 𝒜𝑋removes syntax that acts as zero. This is
a faithful reduction of the action. It does not change any orbit, hull, or computation of seed rank.

The algebraic hull uses finite sums of addressed seed vectors. In the topological setting, taking its clo-

Definition 2.8 (Natural presentation). A seed presentation is natural relative to a declared gram-

system is finite or effectively enumerable, the topology is intrinsic to the realization, no primitive

theorem, or computation not encoded by a primitive chosen for the target.

then calculate those multiplicities.

Finite packet systems give exact coordinates in a direct sum, with no orthogonality requirement.

8 Transfer block algebra and support patterns
A route through this section
Once vectors are resolved into packets, every operator becomes a matrix of maps between packet
spaces. To multiply operators, we sum over the possible intermediate packets. The blocks permit-
ted to be nonzero define a relation on the packet indices. When that relation is a preorder, the
resulting algebra has a triangular structure and a nilpotent ideal of strict transfers.

Scope of the argument
A continuous surjective linear map need not be a quotient map in arbitrary topological vector
spaces. The algebraic first isomorphism theorem gives a bijection on the quotient. A topological
isomorphism requires the quotient topology to agree with the target topology. An applicable open
mapping theorem can supply this agreement, as it does for continuous linear surjections between
Banach spaces.
The completion statement uses the topology transported from the target space. This choice ensures
that approximation in the quotient means approximation in the target. A topology inherited from the
original subspace need not give the same completion unless the two topologies agree. The theorem
therefore names the topology as part of its conclusion.
What we have established
Packet systems transport by conjugation, form a category under packet compatible seeded mor-
phisms, restrict to invariant subspaces, descend to invariant quotients, and survive completion
under explicit boundedness and quotient topology hypotheses.

11.1 Preservation profiles
Definition 11.1 (Realization functor and preservation profile). Let SeedSysabs be an abstract cat-
egory of seed systems and let C𝐷be a domain category. A realization functor is a functor
Ev𝐷∶SeedSysabs ⟶C𝐷
with a declared preservation profile specifying which of the following structures are preserved:
0, 𝐼, finite sums, composition, biproducts,
kernels, cokernels, quotients, tensor products,
packet idempotents, transfer blocks, topological completions.
Preservation of a structure means preservation of its defining identity or universal property, not
merely a similarity of notation.
Theorem 11.2 (Equational realization principle). Let 𝐹∶C →D be an additive functor between
preadditive categories. Any equality of morphisms constructed from declared generating morphisms by finite
sums, additive inverses, identities, zero maps, and composition is preserved by 𝐹. Scalar multiplication
by a coefficient ring is also preserved when the categories are enriched over that ring and 𝐹is linear for
the declared enrichment. If a proof additionally uses a chosen biproduct, kernel, cokernel, quotient, tensor
product, or completion and 𝐹preserves that construction in its declared profile, then the corresponding proof
diagram is transported to D.
Proof. Functoriality gives
𝐹(𝐼) = 𝐼,
𝐹(𝑔∘𝑓) = 𝐹(𝑔) ∘𝐹(𝑓),
and additivity gives
𝐹(0) = 0,
𝐹(𝑓+ 𝑔) = 𝐹(𝑓) + 𝐹(𝑔),
𝐹(−𝑓) = −𝐹(𝑓).
If the declared enrichment is present, linearity additionally gives 𝐹(𝑎𝑓) = 𝑎𝐹(𝑓) for every coefficient 𝑎.
A structural induction on the construction of a morphism expression therefore carries every permitted
equational proof to its image under 𝐹. If a step invokes a universal construction, preservation means
that the image diagram satisfies the same universal property. The uniquely induced morphism in the
source proof is therefore carried to the uniquely induced morphism in the target proof. Repeating this
argument through the finite proof diagram transports the conclusion.
How to read the result
The equational principle covers identities built from operations the functor preserves. Additive
identities require additivity. Identities with scalar coefficients require linear enrichment. Quo-
tients, tensor products, completions, kernels, or limits require their own preservation assump-
tions. The preservation profile records the assumptions needed to carry each step of the proof
into the target category.
11.2 From equation transport to semantic realization
Proposition 11.3 (Realization export principle). Every canonical Paper I identity whose proof uses only the
operations listed in a realization functor’s verified preservation profile remains valid after applying that functor. If
the proof uses a domain specific hypothesis not encoded by the functor, that hypothesis must be verified separately
before the transported statement is promoted to a theorem.
Proof. The first assertion is theorem 11.2. The second is a logical boundary: a functor transports estab-
lished identities and preserved universal constructions, but it does not create an unverified analytic,
topological, positivity, finiteness, or integrality hypothesis.
Definition 11.4 (Semantic realization criterion). A domain theorem is a semantic realization of a
canonical seed calculus theorem only when:
(i) An explicit realization functor or intertwining construction is given.
(ii) The preservation profile covers every construction used in the canonical proof.
(iii) Every additional analytic, finiteness, convergence, positivity, or integrality hypothesis is ver-
ified in the domain.
(iv) The resulting conclusion is stated in the domain’s native objects.
Reuse of the words “seed”, “packet”, or “transfer” without these data is only syntactic reuse.
Scope of the argument
A change of nouns is not a realization theorem. Calling a frequency band, a ramification sector,
and a symmetry sector a “packet” is only terminology until one exhibits the idempotents, proves
reconstruction, identifies the transfer blocks, and checks that the relevant morphisms or limits
preserve those structures.
What we have established
The preservation profile determines which equations and proof constructions pass to a new do-
main. Checking it gives later papers a concrete test for transporting a theorem: identify the real-
ization, check each operation used in the proof, and verify the additional domain hypotheses.

The observed stall is not numerical failure. The associated scalar quotient of dimension two certifies
the lower bound in theorem 6.2. Identifying that quotient with the space that measures geometric
multiplicity is the classical Jordan input stated above.
17 Worked graph model: adjacency algebras
Let 𝐺be a nonempty finite graph with adjacency matrix 𝐴𝐺, and regard 𝕜𝑉(𝐺) as a module over 𝕜[𝐴𝐺].
The general result applies directly to a spectral certificate. For a symmetric real adjacency matrix, the
classical spectral theorem supplies such data.
Within one eigenspace, every polynomial in the adjacency operator acts by a scalar. A seed there-
fore supplies at most one vector direction in that eigenspace. Distinct eigenvalues can be separated by
projector polynomials, so the same seed may supply one direction to each of several eigenspaces. With
a complete eigenbasis, the largest eigenspace determines how many seeds are needed, rather than the
number of distinct eigenvalues.

there are pairwise distinct scalars 𝑎𝜆∈𝕜, multiplicities 𝑚𝜆∈ℕ, and an eigenbasis

𝐴𝐺𝑏𝜆,𝑗= 𝑎𝜆𝑏𝜆,𝑗.

𝕜𝑉(𝐺) = span𝕜{𝑝(𝐴𝐺)𝑠𝑗∶𝑝∈𝕜[𝑡], 1 ≤𝑗≤𝑟} } .

The accompanying Python package is not used as a substitute for proof. It provides exact symbolic
checks and finite numerical regression tests for formulas already proved. The computed ranges and
random seeds are recorded explicitly. These checks do not extend a theorem beyond its hypotheses
or certify an unrestricted numerical implementation. The journal companion also tests integer counts
beyond the precision of floating point arithmetic and rejects the unsupported spectral shortcut for
complex symmetric matrices.

(iii) exact operator reconstruction from all transfer blocks.
(iv) coordinate transport under a dense random similarity transform.
(v) cyclicity of a companion operator.
(vi) the obstruction that requires two seeds for repeated Jordan blocks.
(vii) the semisimple multiplicity formula in representative cases.
(viii) full orbit dimension for two representative nonzero seeds under the full matrix algebra.
(ix) exact reduction and packet multiplication in the elliptic coordinate ring.
(x) seed ranks of path and cycle adjacency modules over the reported finite ranges.

20.2 Diagnostic questions for a new application
Before claiming that a new subject is a realization of Paper I, answer the following.
1. What is the fixed operator grammar or acting algebra?
2. What is the concrete realization space or module?
3. Which seeds are declared before the target is chosen?
4. Is generation algebraic, topological, probabilistic, or approximate?
5. What are the idempotent packets, and in what sense do they sum to the identity?
6. Are the packets finite, countable unconditional, or merely formal?
7. What are the transfer blocks, and which blocks are known to vanish?
8. Which morphisms preserve the packet system?
9. Which quotient, completion, tensor, or limit operations must be preserved?
10. What exact theorem from Paper I is being specialized, and what new domain theorem remains to
be proved?

How to use the paper after the first reading
For a concrete calculation, first reduce the action to the realized algebra. Next compute or bound
seed rank using quotients, the module top, or primary decomposition. Then declare the packet
system and use exact analysis and synthesis. Finally move all operator equations into transfer
blocks, where support, graph, quotient, and functorial constraints become explicit.

23 Conclusions and further use
The results establish the following tools for working with a declared operator action and packet system:
I.1. The two sided annihilator criterion is proved in proposition 3.5.
I.2. Generator detection modulo the Jacobson radical is proved in theorem 5.2.
I.3. The semisimple seed rank formula applies over arbitrary division rings, with the conventions for
left and right modules kept explicit in theorem 5.6.
I.4. The single operator formula and its cyclic criteria apply over arbitrary fields in theorem 6.2
and corollary 6.5.
I.5. The countable unconditional packet theorem is proved in theorem 7.16.
I.6. The classification of support compatible with ∗is proved in corollary 8.14.
I.7. The weighted source component formula gives the packet pure generation requirement under the
propagation hypotheses in theorem 9.7.
I.8. Seed system composition, packet exact sequences, quotient block descent, dense realization, quo-
tient completion, and semantic theorem transport are proved in proposition 10.5, theorems 10.6,
10.10, 10.11 and 11.2, and corollary 10.8.
I.9. Exact sequence bounds, monotonicity under enlargement of the acting algebra, coordinate stabil-
ity, projection onto diagonal blocks, and preorder decomposition are established in theorems 4.6
and 8.15 and propositions 4.3, 7.12 and 8.11.

How to use this volume
Reading route. Exact packet coordinates and residue selectors lead to weighted inversion and
rational walk series. Lattice gluing then gives separation weights and precision delays. Smith con-
gruences and operator defects connect these formulas to finite computation.
Companions. The worked visual atlas appears in this volume and as a separate guide. The Lean
guide distinguishes the current formal development from the inherited 25-row walkthrough. Each
guide records its evidence and scope.
Overview
A complete family of idempotents gives exact coordinates, but a single family does not record
scale or integral visibility. We study towers in which every coarse idempotent is the sum of its fine
descendants. The coordinate changes are invertible and coherent, and every operator block is the
sum of its refined blocks. Residue selectors give a model over arbitrary rings. When roots of unity
are available they agree with character averages, and coprime moduli factor through the Chinese re-
mainder theorem. In a complete filtered algebra, a diagonal operator plus positive weight transfers
has an inverse obtained by summing admissible weighted paths. The formula truncates exactly at
finite precision, while finite transfer graphs have rational path series. For a rational spectral decom-
position over a discrete valuation ring, resultants give denominator bounds. The exact denominator
is the largest Smith exponent of the lattice gluing module. This yields a necessary and sufficient pre-
cision delay, monotonicity under refinement, and a full congruence solving formula. We close with
exact formulas for the propagation of a coarsening defect through powers, resolvents, holomorphic
functions, exponentials, and multilevel towers.
This edition integrates the expanded mathematical narrative with the canonical v1.2.1 certificate level
formulations. It preserves the distinction between general written proofs, formal specifications, and
finite computational examples. The visual atlas and the separate Lean guide provide worked models
and separate current and inherited formal crosswalks.

1 Introduction
A complete family of pairwise annihilating idempotents decomposes a module into exact coordinate
pieces. Many problems require more than one such decomposition. A signal may be split first into
two residue classes and then into four. A filtered operator may be resolved into transfers that appear at
different valuation depths. A rational spectral splitting may exist over the fraction field while remaining
invisible on the original lattice. These are all refinement problems, but they involve different notions
of scale.
The first part of the article concerns exact refinement. If a fine packet family refines a coarse family,
then each coarse idempotent is the sum of its fine descendants. The coordinate spaces at the two levels
are canonically isomorphic because both represent the whole module. The refinement relation adds
more information. It tells us which fine coordinates belong to each coarse coordinate, and it gives a
compatible decomposition of every operator block. This is the algebra behind polyphase coordinates
and nested filter banks. Standard treatments of those subjects may be found in [10, 2].
The second part studies inversion in a complete filtered algebra. Suppose an operator has the form
𝑇= 𝐷+ 𝑁,
where 𝐷is invertible and every packet transfer in 𝑁raises the filtration by a positive amount. The
ordinary Neumann series can then be expanded into weighted paths. The weight is not the number
of edges. It is the total filtration gain along the path. At precision 𝐿, every path of weight at least 𝐿
vanishes. A finite transfer graph also gives a rational generating function for the number of paths of
each total weight. The relevant generating function facts are classical and are discussed in [9].
The third part concerns integral separation. Let 𝑉be a vector space over the fraction field of a discrete
valuation ring 𝒪, and let Λ be an 𝒪lattice in 𝑉. A rational projector 𝐸need not preserve Λ. Its separation

2 Depth and compatibility
Packet, filtration, and separation depths describe three different kinds of scale. Compatibility is initially
recorded by an operator defect. Keeping these notions separate makes the later formulas easier to read.
The first is packet depth. A finer packet family has more idempotents and a more detailed address
set. The passage from residues modulo two to residues modulo four is an example. Packet depth is
combinatorial. It says how many distinctions have been made in the coordinate system.
The second is filtration depth. A transfer in 𝐹𝑟ℬvanishes modulo 𝐹𝑟ℬ. This membership gives a
lower bound on its depth. A nonzero transfer may first become visible only at a higher precision. Two
paths with the same number of edges can have different filtration depths. A longer path can appear
earlier when its edges have smaller weights.
The third is separation depth. A rational packet projector may require multiplication by 𝜋𝑠before it
preserves the chosen lattice. This number depends on both the rational decomposition and the lattice.
It can be zero even when the corresponding eigenvalues are close, and it can be positive even when the
rational projector is simple.
The fourth notion is the compatibility defect. A fine operator and a separately chosen coarse operator
need not commute with coarsening. Their discrepancy is
Δ = 𝐶𝑇𝑓−𝑇𝑐𝐶.
This operator records the failure of one model to represent another exactly. A chosen norm measures
its size, while a chosen filtration can assign a depth. No integer compatibility depth is assigned without
that additional structure.
The four notions meet in applications, but no one of them determines the others. An exact refinement
tower may have zero coordinate error while its fine spectral packets have positive lattice weight. A
filtered inverse may truncate exactly at a given depth while the coarse operator still has a nonzero
compatibility defect. The paper treats each quantity with its own theorem before combining them.
The central idea
Packet depth changes the address of a component. Filtration depth controls when a transfer sur-
vives a precision cutoff. Separation depth clears a rational denominator on a chosen lattice. The
compatibility defect records a discrepancy between two operator models. These quantities can
interact, but each needs its own hypothesis and its own calculation.

The central idea
Word length counts how many transfers are composed. Weight counts how much filtration gain
those transfers guarantee. The sign in the inverse expansion depends on length, while the preci-

a longer word still contributes.

coarse operator may instead be chosen to model coarse dynamics. An intertwining defect measures
the mismatch between applying the operator before or after passing to coarse coordinates.

14 Scope and limits
The exact statements above have several deliberate boundaries.
First, refinement changes coordinates while preserving reconstruction. If a numerical method dis-
cards fine packets, the resulting error must be estimated separately.
Second, the weighted inverse is linear. A nonlinear map creates higher order interactions among
packet coordinates. Those interactions are not contained in the path formula of theorem 5.2.
Third, a resultant is only a denominator bound. The exact weight depends on the lattice and is given
by theorem 8.2. The two examples in examples 7.4 and 8.10 show that the same eigenvalue separation
can give different integral packet weights.
Fourth, the dyadic sign example is a model rather than a classification of all phenomena at the prime
two. Character averages, trace splittings, quadratic refinements, and deformation projectors must each
be checked on their own lattices.
Finally, the defect formulas do not prove that a chosen coarse operator is a good approximation. They
say exactly how a known one step defect propagates. A useful approximation theorem must also bound
that defect in the problem under study.

B.1 Residue analysis and synthesis
def analyze_residues(x, N):
require N > 0
return [x[j::N] for j in range(N)]
def synthesize_residues(packets):
N = len(packets)
require packet lengths fit one N-way interleaving
y = empty(sum(len(p) for p in packets))
for j, packet in enumerate(packets):
y[j::N] = packet
return y

How to use this volume
Begin with typed edge words and exact coordinate transport. A chosen connection introduces
defects, holonomy, and packet obstruction witnesses. Part II develops nonlinear packet jets, tree
expansions, correction complexes, filtered lifting, elimination, and smooth transport.
Part I retains the finite v1.0.1 formal contract. Part II gives the strengthened nonlinear and analytic
development with ordinary proofs. The release also verifies exact nonlinear coordinates, continu-
ous packet jets on actual projector ranges, and the decorated composition and structural support
laws in Lean. The integral Taylor remainder and the later analytic and obstruction results retain
their ordinary proof status. Formal coverage stays attached to the released declarations. The vi-
sual atlas at the end of this volume provides twenty-four worked plates. The separate Lean guide
explains the formal contract and its evidence.
Overview
Finite projector packets turn linear transfer into typed walks and arbitrary maps into exact co-
ordinate representations. Canonical coordinate transport satisfies an exact cocycle law. A chosen
connection can fail to compose, producing holonomy and packet obstruction witnesses. Nonlinear
packet jets lead to higher composition, convergent rooted tree expansions, graded operations, and
nonlinear refinement defects. A specified correction map produces a canonical cokernel obstruction.
Relative exact sequences, mapping cones, Hilbert splitting, nonlinear correction, and filtered lift-
ing describe how these obstructions behave. Exact elimination produces Schur formulas, and finite
transport reduces gluing to fundamental cycle holonomy. For smooth orthogonal packet families,
direct packet rotations converge in operator norm to canonical unitary transport. The finite formal
contract and the broader ordinary proof development retain their separate scopes throughout.
This release presents the mathematical development together with worked examples, a visual atlas, and
a separate guide to the formal proof evidence. The packet norm estimate distinguishes the actual range
jet from its ambient extension. The support statements keep external packet profiles and intermediate
composition witnesses explicitly typed. The accompanying release record gives the exact source and
scope of each formal verification.

1 Purpose and formal status
Paper I fixed typed seeds, operator grammars, exact projector packets, generated hulls, and reconstruc-
tion [13]. Paper II added coherent refinement coordinates, weighted transfer, arithmetic separation,
and linear defect identities [14]. The present paper begins the next layer: explicit edge words, optional
connection data, and obstructions within individual packets.
Canonical coordinate transport and a connection play different mathematical roles. Canonical trans-
port compares two exact descriptions of the same ambient object and is forced by analysis and synthesis.
A connection chooses transports that may carry extra modeling, discretization, or gauge information.
Canonical transport obeys a cocycle theorem. A connection may fail to obey a cocycle, and that fail-
ure is meaningful data. Keeping separate notation lets us distinguish the automatic coherence of exact

13 The finite contract and the nonlinear transition
Typed packet support turns the expansion of a transfer power into a walk calculus. Incompatible words
vanish because their interfaces do not match. Canonical packet coordinate transport is the exact equiv-
alence obtained from analysis and synthesis. It satisfies the cocycle law, so every finite canonical loop
telescopes to the identity. Holonomy enters after a separate connection is supplied. The compiled min-
imal API proves that flatness makes both the relative defect and holonomy trivial, and it exhibits a non-
trivial rational loop. Under the compiled reversible API, a nonzero additive triangle defect is equivalent
to nonidentity holonomy, transforms covariantly under gauge, and is detected exactly by a finite family
of packet blocks. Finite flat paths collapse to their endpoints. Every flat reversible pair connection is
explicitly related to canonical transport by a gauge change through a chosen base chart.
These facts define the boundary of the finite formal contract. At that boundary, exact coordinates
preserve composition and satisfy naturality for arbitrary functions in Paper III, while the typed lin-
ear packet coordinate counterpart remains inherited from Paper II. Nontrivial nonlinear defects must
therefore be attached to additional modeling choices or to packet compatibility of the particular op-
eration. Colored operation trees, multilinear packet labelings, and Faà di Bruno expansions remain
outside this finite Lean contract. Part II develops the corresponding ordinary mathematics, including
packet jets, rooted tree expansions, and explicit nonlinear obstruction theorems.

and holonomy
This part moves from exact coordinates for arbitrary functions to differentiable interactions, specified
correction problems, and finite or smooth transport. Each ordinary proof retains its stated hypotheses.
These results are not asserted to belong to the finite Lean contract of Part I.
The notational change from 𝒜, 𝒮to 𝒜, 𝒮is typographical: both denote analysis and synthesis for the de-
clared packet system. A connection remains additional data. Smooth canonical transport is constructed
from a moving projector family, whereas the algebraic exact coordinate transport in Part I compares

This part develops nonlinear packet representation and the obstruction theory that follows from it.
Exact coordinates preserve a nonlinear problem, but they do not solve it. Once the equation is written

The first stage of Part II treats the local nonlinear calculus. Packet analysis and synthesis conjugate ar-
bitrary maps. Fréchet derivatives split into multilinear packet jets. The higher chain rule then becomes
a Faà di Bruno formula whose terms carry intermediate packet labels. Standard background on Fréchet
calculus and the higher chain rule may be found in [1, 2, 4].
The next stage studies nonlinear iteration. Repeated substitution is indexed by rooted trees rather
than operator words. A scalar majorant gives an absolute convergence theorem for polynomial fixed
point equations. The quadratic case recovers the Catalan series. Rooted tree combinatorics are discussed
in [16, 11, 6].
A linear correction map

versal property and behaves naturally under commuting squares. Mapping cones extend the same
construction to cochain complexes. In a Hilbert space with closed range, the quotient is represented by
the orthogonal projection onto Ker 𝐷∗. The Moore Penrose inverse then gives the least norm correction.
Relevant background appears in [18, 15].
A vanishing linear obstruction is only the first step. We give a contraction theorem for nonlinear
correction, followed by a local Lyapunov Schmidt reduction. In a complete filtered problem, every
lifting step has its own cokernel class. Vanishing at all depths and compatible choices of corrections
produce an exact inverse limit solution. A filtered correction complex carries a spectral sequence. Its
first page records graded obstruction candidates, while later differentials record interactions that can
cancel them. We use the standard spectral sequence of a filtered complex from [18, 12].
The final stage studies elimination and gluing. The implicit function theorem gives an exact Schur
derivative after hidden variables are removed. Finite transport systems reduce, after a spanning tree
gauge, to one holonomy element for each fundamental cycle. The same idea extends to smooth projector
families through Kato transport. We use standard material from [4, 5, 7, 8, 10].
The article does not claim that every nonlinear problem has a finite obstruction space. The cokernel
is canonical only after a correction map has been specified. It may be infinite dimensional. A first order
obstruction may vanish while a higher order obstruction remains. The purpose of the calculus is to
identify the exact object in which each failure lives and to show how those objects change under packets,
refinement, filtration, and transport.
15 A map of the nonlinear calculus
Four questions organize the nonlinear calculus: representation, interaction, correction, and gluing.
The first question is representation. Given a nonlinear map 𝐹, can its packet form be written without
approximation? The answer is yes. Analysis and synthesis are inverse coordinate maps, so conjugation
preserves the full equation.
The second question is interaction. Which input packets influence a given output packet, and at
what derivative order? Packet jets answer this question. They form a directed hypergraph rather than
an ordinary block matrix because one nonlinear interaction can have several inputs.
The third question is correction. Suppose an approximate solution leaves a defect 𝑟. A declared lin-
earized correction map 𝐷removes the part of 𝑟lying in im 𝐷. The quotient class
[𝑟] ∈coker 𝐷
is the part that no allowed first order correction can remove. This quotient class is the obstruction. Its
vanishing must be supplemented by a nonlinear theorem.
The fourth question is gluing. Local coordinate changes can solve every edge problem and still fail
around a loop. The remaining cycle product is holonomy. It measures the failure of a global frame even
when each local equation has been solved.
These four layers fit into the sequence
exact coordinates ⟶packet interactions ⟶correction classes
⟶global gluing.
Each arrow needs hypotheses. Exact coordinates need a complete packet system. Differential inter-
actions need regularity. A cokernel obstruction needs a specified correction map. Holonomy needs
invertible local transports.
A second distinction concerns scale. A refinement defect compares a fine nonlinear model with a
coarse one. It is a point in the coarse output space. An obstruction class is the image of such a defect, or
of another residual, in a quotient by allowed corrections. The correction map must be declared before
the defect determines an obstruction class. A small defect can have a nonzero obstruction, and a large
defect can have zero obstruction if it lies entirely in the correction range.
The paper uses finite packet systems in the coordinate and graph sections. Banach space hypotheses
enter only where norms, contractions, or Fréchet derivatives are used. Module and complex language
is used for cokernels, filtered lifting, and cohomological obstructions. This separation keeps each result
at the level of generality supported by its proof.

Analysis and synthesis undo each other on the complete packet tuple. In a composition of packet

24 Filtered obstruction complexes
A direct packet decomposition splits a complex into independent pieces, so cohomology splits packet
by packet. A filtration retains relations between depths. Its associated graded cohomology can contain
classes that disappear on later pages of a spectral sequence.

depths. Only the first mechanism occurs in a direct sum of subcomplexes. A filtration can exhibit both.

28 Realization data and limits of the calculus
The smooth transport theorem starts with a declared projector family. Applying it to a physical model
requires a construction of that family and, where relevant, a separate continuum limit. Triviality of
holonomy is a further geometric question. The curvature formula in standard fact 27.11 is classical.
Relating it to global holonomy requires geometric information as in [7, 8, 10].
An application begins by specifying the following objects:
1. an ambient nonlinear equation or continuation problem
2. the allowed correction space
3. a linear correction map or a correction complex
4. the defect whose class is to be tested
5. a packet decomposition or filtration compatible with the correction data
6. transition maps between refinement levels
7. transport maps when local solutions must be glued.
Once these objects are fixed, the cokernel and cone constructions are functorial by theorems 21.3
and 21.11. Packet splitting and descent follow from theorem 21.4, proposition 21.6, and corollary 21.12.
Relative loss under coarsening is measured by theorem 21.7.
Filtered lifting follows from theorems 23.2, 23.6 and 23.8. Gluing and comparison of transport sys-
tems follow from theorems 26.4 and 26.6. Smooth packet transport follows from theorems 27.2 and 27.7.
Exact packet coordinates give a representation of the data. Solving the associated problem still re-
quires the correction and lifting hypotheses. The correction map belongs to the problem data, and its
cokernel is canonical relative to that choice. The cokernel may be infinite dimensional. In the Hilbert
setting, the orthogonal obstruction projector requires closed range.
Coarse vanishing can erase a nonzero fine obstruction, and higher nonlinear terms can obstruct
a problem whose linear class vanishes. A spectral sequence records which classes survive the later
differentials. An application of finite graph holonomy or smooth projector transport to a continuum
field theory requires the additional realization data just described.
Whenever a nonlinear continuation problem supplies a correction map, its residual can be recorded
in an exact quotient or cohomology object. Under the stated hypotheses, these objects admit packet de-
composition, filtered refinement, natural transport, and holonomy tests. They identify the obstruction
that a correction or gluing step must address.

How to use this volume
Begin with cyclic projection and the signed differential cycle. The reciprocal chapters then build
parameter polynomials, Appell systems, and theta polynomials from a unit series. The second
half follows the same denominator through large zero geometry, canonical products, and zero
zeta functions.
The visual atlas at the end of this volume supplies twenty-six worked plates. The separate Lean
guide follows the released declarations and their hypotheses. All sixty-eight proof bodies and
ninety-five numbered records of the selected manuscript are retained.
Overview
Fix a positive integer 𝑁. Root of unity projection of the exponential produces residue-class
sections that, for 𝜆≠0, form a basis for 𝑦(𝑁) = 𝜆𝑁𝑦. The signed sections for 𝑦(𝑁) = −𝑦yield
the denominator D𝑁and its reduced form Δ𝑁. We derive reciprocal coefficient polynomials, Bell
and Newton recurrences, an additive parameter law, and residue section Appell and theta families.
For 𝑁≥2, Δ𝑁has order 1/𝑁. We specialize classical two term zero theory for exponential sums to
the regular exponent polygon. In this equal-weight family, conjugation symmetry combined with
unique near-model localization places all sufficiently large zeros exactly on the symmetry rays,
and direct expansion gives their leading displacement and derivative sign. The classical perimeter
law yields zero-counting asymptotics with explicit leading constants and bounded error. These
results give genus zero products, the standard diagonal Fredholm representation, zero-power-sum
formulas for reciprocal and logarithmic coefficients, nearest-zero coefficient asymptotics, and
meromorphic continuation of the symmetry-orbit zero zeta by comparison with the Hurwitz zeta
function. Complex powers are interpreted either formally or through a fixed logarithm on a zero free
domain. The paper treats only this cyclic analytic family. Arithmetic interpolation, general nonlinear
trees, general resolvent theory, and abstract completion are reserved for Papers IX, III, VI, and X.

like manuscript results under their original hypotheses. This volume changes presentation and
adds worked explanations. It does not create a new formal release.
Imported standard fact 11.1 is used in the ordinary manuscript growth argument. The Lean
growth-order proofs establish that step separately. Open questions, branch choices, multiplici-
ties, and the hypotheses of coefficient asymptotics remain explicit. Current finite computations
support the worked models. The compiler and kernel evidence remains the preserved September
release evidence.

reversed sign. The matrix exponential packages every finite path length in one analytic expression.

Part V Scope and formal evidence
15 Scope boundaries and further questions
The large-zero theorem settles eventual simplicity but does not classify the finite exceptional set. A
remaining question is whether every zero of D𝑁is simple and every reduced zero of Δ𝑁is positive.
Both statements hold for 𝑁= 2 and 𝑁= 4. The argument here proves them only outside a compact
set for general 𝑁.
The leading correction in theorem 11.8 may admit iteration to a full exponential expansion for 𝜏𝑚.
Such an expansion is an open problem, not a result of this paper. It could refine the entire correction
in the zero-zeta comparison and lead to explicit special values.
The symmetry-orbit zero zeta has a meromorphic continuation with one pole. No functional
equation is obtained. A branch dependent sum over the 𝑁roots of each reduced zero must specify
logarithms on the rays.
The coefficient families in sections 7, 9 and 10 have exact formal parameter-addition laws. Their arith-
metic behavior, including odd-prime congruences, dyadic weighting, and 𝑝-adic or Amice–Mahler
interpolation, belongs to Paper IX. General bounded-operator semigroup, resolvent, and Feshbach
theory belongs to Paper VI. Paper III owns general nonlinear operation trees, while abstract completion
and occupancy questions belong to Paper X. None of those theories is inferred from the scalar
complex-analytic results proved here.

17 Conclusion
Cyclic projection turns the exponential into a finite differential basis, and the signed cycle produces the
distinguished denominator D𝑁. Its reciprocal powers yield Bell and Newton recurrences, an additive
parameter law, Appell systems, and theta polynomials. Reduction by 𝑤= 𝑧𝑁then connects the
reciprocal coefficients to a genus zero product and reduced-zero power sums.
Classical two term localization, specialized to the regular exponent polygon and combined with
reflection symmetry, places all sufficiently large zeros on symmetry rays. The displacement, derivative
and counting estimates yield the family-specific Hurwitz comparison for the orbit zero zeta.

Part I: The released formal core
Coordinates first, decisions second
A residue decomposition changes the coordinates of a signal without changing its information.
Filtering then acts between those coordinates. Approximation enters when an operator compresses
a component or when a decision discards coefficients. The formal core follows these operations in
that order.
Overview
This paper develops the signal realization of the projector-resolved seed calculus. The impulse
𝛿0 is taken as a primitive signal seed and its shift orbit supplies the address system. Residue pro-
jectors split a sequence into exact polyphase channels, nested divisibility gives exact refinement,
and every finite impulse-response operator becomes a matrix of packet transfers. The standard
perfect-reconstruction condition for a filter bank is therefore an analysis–synthesis identity in the
common operator language of the series. Haar analysis and every finite-depth wavelet-packet trans-
form are treated on complex ℓ2, together with concrete finite-signal models and a predict–update
lifting step. The edge problem is separated into two statements. When a discontinuity packet is
known and retained exactly, approximation error is exactly the approximation error of the remain-
ing smooth packet. No spectral approximation of the jump is performed. When the packet is esti-
mated, a symmetric-difference bound isolates mask error, amplitude error, and smooth-background
error. Numerical studies compare global Fourier truncation, exact known-packet reconstruction,
and a deliberately narrow positive-contrast estimator in one and two dimensions, including curved
boundaries, corners, and multiple amplitudes. The same cyclic phase action is then placed on the
Smith reflection disk. Its pullback through the Cayley transform is a Möbius action on impedance,
and the two-phase case is precisely impedance–admittance inversion. Nonlinear coefficient prod-
ucts obey cyclic packet convolution. The preserved September 2026 release integrates a Lean for-
malization of all twenty theorem-like statements under the hypotheses stated below: 225 supporting
theorem targets in 23 modules. Eighteen regenerated figures, machine-readable numerical results,
the 33-test original companion suite, and 36 additional exact-model and verifier tests accompany
the paper. Exact signal theorems, limited numerical estimators, classical constructions, and open
recovery problems are kept distinct throughout.
Scope and claim boundary
The paper proves exact polyphase reconstruction, exact finite filter-transfer identities, perfect re-
construction for the stated filter banks, the conditional known-edge theorem, mask and amplitude
perturbation bounds, nonlinear residue-convolution laws, and the Smith-coordinate phase action.
It does not claim that every discontinuity can be detected automatically, that every form of Gibbs
ringing has been eliminated, or that the simple two-class estimator supplied with the release is a
universal segmentation method. The estimator is included as one reproducible finite example. For
every finite packet refinement tree, the paper now proves existence of a globally optimal complete
pruning, an exact dynamic-programming selector for additive costs, and a deterministic margin-
stability certificate. Wavelets, filter banks, the Cayley transform, and the classical Smith grid are
treated as classical inputs organized in the common seed–packet–refinement language.
Verification convention. “Lean-checked” refers to the explicitly scoped theorem statements and their
supporting declarations, accepted by the pinned Lean kernel. It does not certify the English text au-
tomatically, the floating-point Python implementation, physical modelling choices, or the two con-
jectures. The manuscript-to-declaration correspondence has been reviewed manually. Appendix D
records it result by result. The September 2026 release records a rerun of the numerical experiments.
The current final-edition checks are distinguished in the opening reading note.

D.3 Three bridges that matter for the statement
Finite filters and numerical transforms.
The filter-bank proof is an algebraic theorem about finite
Laurent-polynomial kernels acting faithfully on bilateral sequences. Equality at a single complex value
of 𝑧would be insufficient to prove a polynomial identity; the impulse argument avoids that error. The
separate transform theorem proves the finite-filter action agrees with evaluation wherever the weighted
input series converge absolutely. An arbitrary bilateral ℓ2 sequence need not have an absolutely con-
vergent numerical 𝑧-transform. The all-sequence time-domain theorem makes no such assumption.
Recursive trees and set-valued prunings.
The formal tree permits any positive finite arity at an inter-
nal node, including arity one. A node has a position in the tree, so equal data labels on distinct nodes
do not identify the nodes. A recursive cut is either a stop or a collection of child cuts. Its equivalence
with a covering antichain is proved in both directions. The cost, envelope, and operator sums are then
shown to equal actual finite sums over the selected node set. This connects the recursive optimizer to
the manuscript’s set-valued definition instead of assuming that connection.
Hilbert operators and finite experiments.
The coordinate maps, literal Haar channels, and packet
operators are constructed on complex ℓ2. Square summability and boundedness are established be-
fore adjoints are used. The finite Python experiments separately check indexing, reconstruction, and
energy at finite lengths. They illustrate these operators but are not the objects executed by the Lean ker-
nel. Likewise, the Python Smith routine evaluates only finite charts; the Lean projective construction
supplies the pole-safe universal statement.

Part II: Extended mathematical development
Multiresolution Signal Calculus, Singular Packets, and Stable Reconstruction
This part preserves the complete standalone mathematical branch, with the explicit audit repairs
recorded in the accompanying source ledger. Its sixty-three proofs are prose proofs; no additional Lean
coverage is asserted. Section and result numbers carry the prefix E to distinguish this scope from Part
I.
Overview
Signals on a lattice admit exact coordinates indexed by the residue classes of every finite index
sublattice. Convolution becomes a matrix of packet transfers, while filter banks and packet trees
become exact changes of coordinates. We develop this structure on sequence spaces, prove quantita-
tive stability for imperfect and perturbed banks, and give an exact dynamic recursion for adaptive
packet trees. A singular signal is written as a smooth component plus step or truncated power pack-
ets that record jumps in the signal and its derivatives. Retaining the correct packets leaves only the
smooth approximation error. Estimated packets are governed by exact formulas involving value er-
ror, region overlap, boundary displacement, and the norm of the smooth approximation operator.
The main recovery result treats separated jumps sampled on a uniform grid. An explicit contrast gap
gives exact recovery of every jump cell, grid scale location accuracy, amplitude control, and finite
norm consistency. Probability bounds cover sub Gaussian noise and repeated measurements. Haar
coefficients, two shifted grids, and annihilating differences give complementary localization results.
The final sections treat Gibbs oscillation, nonlinear residue interactions, numerical illustrations, and
cyclic Cayley coordinates.
E1 Introduction
Polyphase decompositions, filter banks, lifting schemes, and wavelet packets are standard parts
of multirate signal processing and harmonic analysis. Their classical development is described in
[CR83, Vai93, VK95, SN96, Dau92, Mal09]. These theories are often introduced through several parallel
languages. Residue classes appear in polyphase analysis. Matrix symbols appear in filter banks. Trees
appear in wavelet packets. Singularities are handled through a different approximation or detection
method. The first aim of this article is to place these constructions in one exact coordinate system.
The second aim is to separate representation from recovery. If a signal has already been written as

estimated singular packet. The third is the amplification caused by applying a reconstruction operator

The latter encode jumps in derivatives of order 𝑚. They permit a piecewise smooth function to be

of the informal statement that a discontinuity should be represented directly rather than approximated
by a global smooth basis.
The recovery theory begins with one dimensional separated jumps. For bounded deterministic noise,
thresholding adjacent sample contrasts recovers the exact grid cells containing the jumps whenever
the jump size exceeds the combined smooth variation and noise by an explicit margin. The same proof
gives location and amplitude bounds. A sub Gaussian version follows from a union bound. Averaging
repeated measurements reduces the required threshold in the expected way. Haar coefficients provide
a second detection mechanism. Two grids shifted by half a cell guarantee that every jump is well placed
in at least one grid, which removes the most elementary dyadic alignment failure.
The literature on singularity detection is much broader than the results proved here. Wavelet modu-
lus maxima are developed in [MH92]. Best basis selection in packet libraries was introduced in [CW92].
Nonlinear approximation is surveyed in [DeV98]. Geometric image models, wedgelets, and curvelets
appear in [Don99, CD04]. The present article does not replace those theories. Its narrower purpose is
to give a common exact calculus in which coordinate reconstruction, adaptive basis selection, singular
packet estimation, and smooth approximation remain logically separate.
The article is organized as follows. Appendices E2 and E3 develop lattice addresses and exact residue
coordinates in any dimension. Appendices E4 and E5 express convolution and filter banks in those
coordinates, including stability under imperfect reconstruction and filter perturbation. Appendix E6
treats arbitrary pruned packet trees and stability of the best basis decision. Appendices E7 and E8
introduce step and higher order singular packets, exact reconstruction identities, and error formulas.
Appendices E9 and E10 prove deterministic and probabilistic recovery results. Appendices E11 and E12
treat Gibbs oscillation and nonlinear interactions. The final sections record finite numerical illustrations
and a secondary cyclic Cayley realization.
Several conclusions are deliberately excluded. The paper does not prove a universal image segmen-
tation theorem. Exact recovery of separated jumps in one dimension does not imply stable recovery
of arbitrary boundaries in higher dimensions. Retaining a correct singular packet does not remove
noise or model error. An adaptive tree selected by an additive objective need not remain optimal when
global hardware costs or cross packet interactions are introduced. The Cayley coordinate section is a
secondary conformal realization and is not used in the recovery theorems.

E15 Limits and further directions
The one dimensional recovery theorem identifies an explicit admissible threshold interval for an ad-
jacent contrast detector. More general recovery requires a broader observation model. A multiscale
average can reduce fixed sample noise, but its bias depends on the smoothness class and the separa-
tion of nearby jumps. A useful next theorem should select the averaging scale from the data while
retaining a finite probability certificate.
Higher dimensional recovery requires geometry. The overlap and tube formulas in appendix E8
become quantitative once a boundary estimate is known. What remains is a stable method that recov-
ers topology, orientation, curvature, and region values under a declared noise model. Wedgelets and
curvelets show why directional geometry is essential for broad image classes [Don99, CD04].
The best basis recursion is exact for additive objectives. Cross packet leakage, shared computation,
and global hardware constraints introduce couplings between subtrees. Those problems require a
larger compiler or an approximation theorem. The cost stability results in theorem E6.6 and corol-
lary E6.7 identify one condition under which the additive decision survives perturbation.
The higher order singular packet theorem removes finitely many trace jumps. A more complete ap-
proximation theory should connect packet norms to geometric measure quantities in BV, piecewise
Sobolev spaces, and free discontinuity models. It should also determine when a redundant packet dic-
tionary can identify the derivative order of a singularity rather than merely its location.
Finally, the two shifted Haar grids remove one exact alignment failure, but they are redundant. A
complete redundant theory should provide stable synthesis, noise aware coefficient aggregation, and
a best basis rule that does not count the same singularity several times.
E16 Conclusion
Finite index sublattices give exact coordinates for lattice signals. In those coordinates, convolution is a
matrix of transfer kernels. Perfect reconstruction is a matrix inverse identity. Approximate reconstruc-
tion is controlled by a multiplier norm. Frame bounds are pointwise singular value bounds. Lifting
steps are exact triangular coordinate changes. Every admissible packet tree gives a complete coordi-
nate system, and every additive tree objective has an exact dynamic recursion.
The singular packet theory separates representation from recovery. A finite family of truncated pow-
ers records jumps in a function and its derivatives, leaving a globally Sobolev remainder under explicit
trace assumptions. If the packet is known and retained, the error is exactly the smooth approximation
error. If the packet is estimated, exact region overlap and location formulas quantify the remaining
defect, while the reconstruction operator contributes a transparent stability factor.
For separated one dimensional jumps, a deterministic contrast gap gives exact cell recovery, midpoint
location accuracy, and amplitude control. A sub Gaussian version follows from one union bound, and
repeated measurements reduce the effective noise scale. Haar coefficients provide a second separation
law because smooth coefficients decay one full power of scale faster than jump coefficients. Two shifted
grids remove boundary alignment at a fixed scale. Higher differences annihilate piecewise polynomial
interiors and confine their response to breakpoint bands.
The resulting chain is
lattice coordinates ⟶transfer blocks ⟶stable filter banks ⟶packet trees
⟶singular packet model ⟶local recovery ⟶smooth approximation rate.
Every arrow is exact or quantitatively controlled under the hypotheses stated in the corresponding
result.

Part I
The released formal core
Projector-Resolved Seed Calculus VI
Transfer Semigroups: Stochastic, Bayesian, Fractional, and PDE Realizations
Overview
This paper develops the transfer-semigroup realization of the projector-resolved seed calculus.
A seed is propagated by a one-parameter semigroup, a Markov kernel, a normalized Bayesian trans-
fer, a fractional spectral power, a Green operator, or a potential-weighted Feynman–Kac operator.
Exact packet projectors resolve every transfer into input-output blocks, and the semigroup law be-
comes block convolution over intermediate packets. Coarse and fine generators are compared by a
refinement defect. A Duhamel identity proves that this generator-level defect is exactly the source
of the corresponding semigroup defect and gives a quantitative stability bound. In the stochastic
realization, point-mass seeds generate random walks and continuous-time Markov evolution; ex-
act lumpability is the vanishing of the same refinement defect. Conditional expectation is treated
as a weighted orthogonal packet projector, with nested partitions producing martingale-difference
packets. Bayesian conditioning is a normalized nonlinear operator. Its independent-data composi-
tion law, packet-evidence decomposition, stability bound, conjugate updates, and continuous likeli-
hood flow are proved explicitly. The Bayesian refinement conjecture is resolved in finite dimensions:
for strictly positive likelihoods and at least two coarse packets, exact commutation for every prior
is equivalent to blockwise-constant likelihoods up to global scale, and every failure factors through
an explicit information-loss packet. Fractional powers are constructed packetwise through the spec-
tral projectors of a positive operator, and the square-root semigroup is recovered by subordination.
The fractional-naturality conjecture is also resolved for bounded nonnegative self-adjoint refinement
systems: the fractional intertwining defect has an exact resolvent integral, a gap-free Hölder cer-
tificate, a sharper common-gap estimate, and a Duhamel semigroup bound. Green kernels, finite-
difference Poisson problems, and second-order low-mode convergence provide the PDE realization.
A finite-state Feynman–Kac formula is proved by path enumeration. Exact Schur–Feshbach elim-
ination shows that discarded latent packets return as a frequency-dependent self-energy and, in
time coordinates, as a memory kernel. Survival and hazard functions are generated by transient
semigroups. Nineteen code-generated figures, machine-readable results, the original thirty-seven
automated tests, and seventeen added boundary-case checks accompany this reviewed edition. The
inherited September 6 release records five checked Lean blocks covering all 33 scoped theorem-like
results in Appendix A. Finite-dimensional theorems, classical infinite-dimensional extensions, nu-
merical certificates, and open continuum claims are kept separate.
Scope and claim boundary. The paper proves the stated finite-dimensional semigroup, packet,
Markov, Bayesian, conditional-expectation, fractional spectral, Green-kernel, Feynman–Kac,
Schur–Feshbach, and survival identities. It also proves quantitative refinement-defect formu-
las under explicit norm hypotheses, including exact transfer of a bounded generator defect to
every fractional power 0 < 𝛼< 1 for bounded nonnegative self-adjoint generators. It does not
claim that an arbitrary infinite-dimensional operator generates a semigroup, that every stochas-
tic process admits a finite packet representation, that every posterior family is conjugate, that
finite Bayesian sufficiency automatically extends to infinite disintegrations, or that every PDE
continuum limit follows from a finite test. Domain, closability, sectoriality, measurability, tight-
ness, and compactness hypotheses remain necessary in their respective infinite-dimensional
settings. Classical sources are retained in the separate end-of-series reference ledger rather than
reproduced in this paper.

17 Remaining conjectural extensions
The finite theory closes several operator identities but does not settle the corresponding universal con-
tinuum questions.
Conjecture 17.1 (Transfer-semigroup realization). Every sufficiently regular realization of the seed cal-
culus whose transfer stage is local in time admits a closed generator on a completed state space, and
the packet analysis maps form a compatible system for its semigroup or evolution family.
Conjecture 17.2 (Uniform refinement control). For a nested family of physically or analytically mean-
ingful discretizations, there exist norms and constants independent of resolution such that
∥𝐶ℓ𝑒𝑡𝐴ℓ+1 −𝑒𝑡𝐴ℓ𝐶ℓ∥≤𝑀𝑡‖𝐶ℓ𝐴ℓ+1 −𝐴ℓ𝐶ℓ‖
on every bounded time interval. Summable generator defects would then produce a coherent inverse-
limit evolution.
Conjecture 17.3 (Latent-packet closure). For a stable infinite packet system, exact elimination of unre-
solved packets produces a causal memory kernel whose Laplace transform is the limiting packet self-
energy. A Markovian closure exists precisely when this self-energy is constant, or can be represented
by finitely many additional state packets.
Boundary 17.4 (What remains outside Paper VI). The following issues are not proved here:
1. existence and uniqueness for arbitrary stochastic differential equations;
2. posterior consistency or asymptotic normality in infinite statistical models;
3. domain invariance for unbounded fractional operators;
4. tightness and compactness required for stochastic continuum limits;
5. nonlinear PDE well-posedness beyond the stated finite and linear models;
6. an optimal packet choice for a general Markov, Bayesian, or PDE problem.
These belong to later realization-specific work or to external analytic theory.

19 Conclusion
The transfer-semigroup realization gives one common operator language to several subjects that are
often presented separately. Markov propagation is linear transfer of a probability seed. Conditional ex-
pectation is stochastic projection. Bayesian conditioning is normalized nonlinear transfer, and its exact
finite coarsening law is now characterized by packetwise likelihood sufficiency. Fractional calculus is
spectral packet reweighting, and bounded positive refinement defects now transfer to fractional powers
and fractional semigroups by explicit resolvent and Duhamel estimates. A Green operator reconstructs
a field from source packets. Feynman–Kac propagation adds path weights to stochastic transfer. Schur–
Feshbach elimination shows that hidden packets are not destroyed; they return through self-energy and
memory. Survival and hazard are scalar reconstructions of a transient semigroup.
The central structural identity is
generator defect ⟶Duhamel semigroup defect ⟶controlled refinement error.
Together with exact packet reconstruction, this makes the semigroup paper the natural bridge from the
foundational calculus to the quantum, computational, and arithmetic realizations that follow.

Part II
Extended mathematical development
Overview
A bounded generator and a finite packet system turn a semigroup into a matrix of transfer blocks.
We prove convolution, differential, path, Laplace, resolvent, and defect formulas. Exact intertwin-
ing yields an inverse limit semigroup. Weighted summable adjacent defects give convergent recon-
structed evolutions, while range leakage determines whether the limit remains a semigroup. For
finite Markov chains we identify a canonical lumping obstruction and quantify its failure. Condi-
tional expectations give orthogonal martingale packets, and the Ornstein Uhlenbeck semigroup
gives a countable Hermite model. Bayesian updating is treated as normalized transfer. We char-
acterize exact coarse sufficiency, determine the coarsest nontrivial fixed sufficient partition for a
likelihood family when the common level sets are nontrivial, and split relative information into
coarse and local terms. Positive fractional powers are handled through spectral, Balakrishnan, and
subordination formulas. Green operators, finite differences, and finite state Feynman Kac formulas
provide analytic realizations. Schur Feshbach elimination produces a rational self energy and an
exact memory kernel. Every stable finite hidden system yields a polynomial exponential expansion,
including Jordan blocks. A certified optimal primary block selection and a Volterra estimate control
reduced trajectories. State dependent killing, survival laws, moments, and competing risks complete
the finite theory.
E1 Introduction
One parameter semigroups provide a common language for evolution equations, Markov processes,
diffusion, and resolvent methods. Standard analytic foundations appear in [Paz83, EN00]. Finite
Markov chains and their coarse descriptions are treated in [KS60, Nor97, RP81]. Conditional expec-
tation and martingale difference decompositions are basic parts of probability theory [Wil91]. Gaus-
sian transfer and Hermite expansions provide a spectral model for the Ornstein Uhlenbeck semigroup
[Jan97]. Fractional powers of generators and subordinate semigroups belong to the functional calculus
of positive and sectorial operators [Bal60, SSV12]. The Feynman Kac formula, projection methods, and
phase type laws add three further views of transfer [Kac49, Fes58, Zwa61, Neu81].
These subjects share a simple operation. A state is propagated, resolved into declared components,
compared across levels, and reconstructed. The same operation can be linear, as in a Markov semi-
group, or normalized and nonlinear, as in Bayesian conditioning. Hidden components can be discarded
from the state vector without disappearing from the dynamics. Their exact influence returns through
a frequency dependent self energy or a time dependent memory kernel.
The first part of the article treats bounded semigroups on Banach spaces. A finite packet system
resolves every operator into input and output blocks. The semigroup law becomes block convolution.
Splitting the generator into its packet diagonal and transfer part gives a convergent Dyson expansion
over directed packet paths. For a coarse map 𝐶, the generator defect
Δ = 𝐶𝐴𝑓−𝐴𝑐𝐶
produces the entire semigroup defect through a Duhamel integral. The same defect controls resolvents
and holomorphic functions of the generators.
The next question concerns refinement towers. Exact intertwining gives a coordinatewise semigroup
on the bounded inverse limit. Approximate refinement is more delicate. Even if every adjacent defect
is small, reconstruction from a fine level can introduce a second error because a coarse state need not
remain inside the reconstructed fine subspace. We separate these two effects. Summability of adjacent
defects gives a uniform limit of reconstructed coarse evolutions. An asymptotic closure condition is
then sufficient for the limiting family to satisfy the semigroup law.
The probabilistic part begins with finite Markov chains. Exact lumpability is the vanishing of a canon-
ical obstruction on the kernel of aggregation. In coordinates, this is equality of the transition mass sent
from any two states in the same source block into every target block. The usual finite horizon defect
formula follows from telescoping. Conditional expectation is then treated as an orthogonal projector.
A nested family of partitions produces mutually orthogonal martingale packets and an exact energy
decomposition.
Bayesian updating requires more care because normalization depends on the current prior. Given a
partition, every fine update has an exact two stage description. The block masses are updated by prior
dependent average likelihoods, while the conditional distribution inside each block is updated by its
centered likelihood variation. A fixed coarse Bayesian rule works for every prior precisely when the
likelihood is constant inside each block. This gives a finite and exact form of Bayesian sufficiency. For
a family of likelihoods with at least two common level sets, those level sets form the unique coarsest
nontrivial fixed sufficient partition. Relative entropy then separates exactly into information retained
by the coarse packet masses and information carried by the local conditional changes. The same part
derives perturbation bounds, the replicator flow, a variance identity for accumulated evidence, and
stability estimates for hidden Markov filtering.
For a positive operator 𝐿, spectral packets define 𝐿𝛼and e−𝑡𝐿𝛼. Exact intertwining passes to every
fractional power. When both fine and coarse operators have a common positive lower bound 𝑚, the
Balakrishnan formula gives the quantitative estimate

The final sections move from generators to source reconstruction and hidden variables. The one
dimensional Dirichlet Green kernel is reproduced exactly by the scaled inverse of the second difference

smooth Poisson solutions. Finite state Feynman Kac transfer is proved in discrete and continuous time.
Schur Feshbach elimination yields the exact projected resolvent, the retained memory equation, and

E4 Refinement towers and limiting evolution
How to read the result
The limiting argument names its topology, reconstruction maps, and summability weights. Con-
vergence of reconstructed trajectories is distinct from closure under the semigroup law. The range-
leakage condition identifies the additional obstruction to that closure.
The exact inverse limit and the approximate completion problem require different hypotheses. Exact
intertwining preserves the inverse limit coordinate by coordinate. Approximate intertwining gives a
Cauchy family only after reconstruction maps are chosen.

E18 Limits and further questions
The bounded inverse limit theorem isolates one clean route to continuum evolution. Unbounded gen-
erators require graph norms, domain compatibility, and a generation theorem. The range leakage the-
orem converts the closure quantity into an off diagonal generator estimate for bounded orthogonal
refinement models. Concrete discretizations still require a uniform estimate for that off diagonal block.
The finite Bayesian sufficiency theorem is exact, but it concerns one likelihood and one fixed partition.
The relative entropy chain rule measures both retained and discarded information for that update.
Statistical sufficiency for a parametric family requires a common packet structure that preserves the
full parameter dependence. In continuous models the corresponding object is a sufficient sigma algebra
or statistic.
The fractional defect theorem uses a common spectral gap. Removing that gap requires weaker
norms or a Hölder estimate near the null space. For sectorial operators, the same calculation should be
carried out through resolvent bounds on a sector, with domains tracked explicitly. The finite spectral
statement does not settle those issues.
The Green and Poisson results exploit a one dimensional second difference matrix. Higher dimen-
sions, irregular meshes, and variable coefficients require a separate stability theory. The packet lan-
guage remains useful only after coercivity, consistency, and boundary approximation have been estab-
lished.
Memory compression is exact once a finite hidden realization is known and quantitative once an
integrable kernel approximation is supplied. The primary decomposition shows that a finite hidden
block always produces polynomial exponential modes, including the effects of Jordan chains. Choosing
a short approximation remains a different problem. Strongly nonnormal systems can exhibit transient
growth and may require balanced or rational approximation methods. General Volterra kernels need
not admit a short finite realization.
Finally, Markov lumping, Bayesian sufficiency, and memory closure answer different questions.
Lumpability asks whether coarse probabilities evolve autonomously. Bayesian sufficiency asks
whether a fixed coarse likelihood reproduces the posterior packet masses without hiding a change
in the conditional distribution inside a packet. Memory closure asks whether discarded dynamics can
be represented without history. Similar notation should not obscure these distinctions.
E19 Conclusion
A bounded semigroup becomes a matrix of packet transfers once a finite packet system is fixed. The
matrix obeys convolution in time, a closed differential system, a Laplace resolvent formula, and a di-
rected path expansion. A generator defect propagates through Duhamel’s formula and through the
resolvent calculus. Exact compatibility gives a semigroup on the bounded inverse limit. Summable
adjacent defects give convergent reconstructed evolutions. Range leakage, and in particular an off di-
agonal generator block, determines whether the limit retains the semigroup law.
In probability, the same structure appears in several forms. Markov transfer is linear and exact
lumpability is the vanishing of a canonical kernel obstruction. Conditional expectation is an orthogonal
stochastic projector whose differences form martingale packets. The Ornstein Uhlenbeck semigroup
resolves exactly into Hermite packets. Bayesian transfer is nonlinear because of evidence normaliza-
tion. Its exact two stage decomposition separates coarse packet evidence from local conditional change.
Relative entropy then records exactly how much information lies at each level. A fixed sufficient coarse
description exists for every prior precisely when the likelihood is constant inside each packet. The
common level sets of a likelihood family give its unique coarsest fixed sufficient partition.
Positive fractional powers preserve exact intertwining. Under a common spectral gap, the Balakr-
ishnan formula turns an ordinary generator defect into an explicit fractional defect. Green operators
and finite differences show how source reconstruction fits the same transfer language. Feynman Kac
weights Markov paths by a potential without leaving the semigroup framework.
Hidden packets provide the final structural lesson. Exact elimination does not erase them. It re-
turns them as a rational self energy in the resolvent and a causal memory kernel in time. The primary
decomposition of the hidden generator produces every finite memory kernel as a finite sum of poly-
nomial exponential modes. Stable blocks can be truncated with an integrated error certificate, and the
Volterra estimate transfers that certificate to the retained trajectory. State dependent killing identifies
the Feynman Kac potential with a survival mechanism. Survival and competing risks are then scalar
reconstructions of a transient semigroup.
The article therefore separates four operations that are often compressed into one informal idea of
coarse dynamics:
intertwining ⟶refinement control
⟶statistical sufficiency
⟶memory closure.
Each arrow has its own hypotheses and its own obstruction.
